# Controls on tectonic accretion versus erosion in subduction zones: Implications for the origin and recycling of the continental crust

## Key takeaways

### Takeaway 1

**Summary:** Whether a convergent margin is accretionary or erosive is controlled primarily by convergence rate and trench-sediment thickness.

- **Background:** Active margins were traditionally viewed as sites of sediment accretion, but seismic surveys, drilling, forearc subsidence, and exposed igneous or mantle rocks demonstrated widespread nonaccretion and removal of overriding-plate basement (Hussong and Uyeda, 1981; von Huene and Lallemand, 1990; von Huene and Scholl, 1991). The paper therefore classifies margins by net forearc growth or loss over periods longer than 10 Myr, not simply by the presence of a small frontal prism. (PDF pp. 1–3)
- **Result:** The global compilation shows that accretionary margins generally have forearc slopes below 3°, orthogonal convergence below 7.6 cm/yr, and/or trench sediment thicker than 1 km, whereas erosion is favored above $6.0\pm0.1$ cm/yr and with less than 1 km of sediment (Figures 3, 7–10). Fifty-seven percent of active margins are classified as erosive. (PDF pp. 8, 14–18, 26–27)
- **Discussion:** Faster convergence both steepens forearc wedges, probably through higher basal friction, and reduces the residence time available to accumulate trench sediment; thick sediment supplies more fluid and favors shallow accretionary tapers, but convergence rate is interpreted as the dominant first-order control. (PDF pp. 16–19, 26)

### Takeaway 2

**Summary:** Sediment accretion is inefficient, so both accretionary and erosive margins transfer large volumes of crustal material beneath the forearc.

- **Background:** Earlier global analysis suggested that even accretionary margins subduct about 70% of their sediment column, implying substantial recycling of continent-derived material through arcs or into the mantle (von Huene and Scholl, 1991); sediment contributions to arc magma are independently widespread (Woodhead and Fraser, 1985; Tera et al., 1986; Plank and Langmuir, 1993). (PDF pp. 1–3)
- **Result:** Only 7–37% of incoming sediment is accreted, with a global median of 17%; thus about 83% passes at least approximately 50 km beneath accretionary forearcs. In erosive margins, sediment supplies only 12–48% (median 22%) of the total deeply subducted material because eroded forearc basement dominates their budgets (Figures 9 and 12). (PDF pp. 16, 18, 20–21)
- **Discussion:** Accretion efficiency decreases broadly with convergence rate and may also favor sandy trench sections, but it is not simply related to sediment thickness. Consequently, accretionary margins are major deep-subduction pathways as well as sites of net forearc growth. (PDF pp. 18–21, 26)

### Takeaway 3

**Summary:** Long-term forearc erosion has no simple steady first-order control; episodic collision of major oceanic ridges is the strongest identified accelerator.

- **Background:** Tectonic erosion has been linked to plate coupling, abrasion, and possibly high fluid pressure, while subsidence histories and trenchward migration of formerly shallow deposits provide long-term retreat estimates (Hilde, 1983; von Huene and Lallemand, 1990; Lallemand, 1995, 1998; von Huene and Ranero, 2003). (PDF pp. 2–6)
- **Result:** Trench-retreat rate shows no clear correlation with convergence rate, sediment thickness or delivery, or subducting-plate age (Figure 11). Documented ridge collisions more than double long-term erosion at Tonga, increase retreat eightfold in Peru, and raise erosion along Chile and Costa Rica, although slower continuous erosion also occurs without ridge collision. (PDF pp. 18–20)
- **Discussion:** The authors infer that subducting-plate roughness—especially episodic aseismic-ridge collision—dominates long-term erosion histories, while normal rough oceanic basement alone appears unable to sustain the fastest retreat rates. (PDF pp. 19–20, 26)

### Takeaway 4

**Summary:** Arc magmatism, distributed mainly according to convergence rate, must balance large tectonic losses and dominates the creation of new crust at active margins.

- **Background:** Active-margin magmatism is regarded as a principal source of continental crust (Dewey and Windley, 1981; Taylor and McLennan, 1985; Rudnick and Fountain, 1995; Barth et al., 2000), yet the earlier global estimate of 20–40 km³ Myr⁻¹ km⁻¹ of arc growth is below the loss rate derived here (Reymer and Schubert, 1984). Nearly constant Phanerozoic freeboard has instead been interpreted to require slow net continental growth (Schubert and Reymer, 1985; Jacobsen, 1988). (PDF pp. 1, 21–22)
- **Result:** Maintaining current continental volume requires average arc productivity of about 90 km³ Myr⁻¹ km⁻¹, or 91 km³ Myr⁻¹ km⁻¹ with slow growth. Scaling melt production by melting-column height gives geologically implausible arc budgets (Figure 14), whereas scaling it by convergence rate gives more plausible results and makes magmatism 55–95% of growth at accretionary margins (Figure 15). Several oceanic erosive arcs still grow because fast convergence drives melt production faster than tectonic erosion removes crust (Figures 15–16). (PDF pp. 21–26)
- **Discussion:** Convergence rate is favored over melting-column height as the long-term control on melt production. Stable oceanic arcs require a balance among melt supply, crustal thickness, and trench retreat; at 8 cm/yr convergence and 3 km/Myr retreat, crust thicker than 36 km would undergo net loss. (PDF pp. 23–27)

### Takeaway 5

**Summary:** The global budget implies rapid continental-crust recycling and requires oceanic-arc accretion to offset loss at erosive continental margins.

- **Background:** Subduction zones are the only major route by which continental material can return to great depth, so balancing sediment subduction, tectonic erosion, and arc output is essential to models of continental-crust origin and survival. Isotopic models span substantial recycling to early rapid crustal growth followed by slower growth (Armstrong, 1971, 1981; Allègre and Rousseau, 1984; Taylor and McLennan, 1985). (PDF pp. 1, 22)
- **Result:** Forearc basement accounts for about 55% of deeply subducted crustal material, exceeding sediment subduction by roughly 20%; at the calculated loss rate, a volume equal to modern continental crust passes through subduction zones every 2.2 Gyr (Figures 17–18). Oceanic arcs grow overall, but several continental arcs—including South America, Kamchatka, and the Philippines—lose crust (Figure 16). (PDF pp. 24–27)
- **Discussion:** Maintaining continental volume requires growing oceanic arcs eventually to accrete to continents. Much subducted continental material is inferred to pass deeper than shallow arc recycling, while new mantle-derived magmatism replenishes crust; oceanic plateaus are considered a minor contributor, and arc collision may chemically transform initially mafic arc crust into more suitable continental building blocks (Draut et al., 2002). (PDF pp. 25–27)

## Figure summaries

### Figure 1

**Summary:** Schematics contrast accretionary margins, built from deformed off-scraped sediment, with erosive margins, where steep igneous or mantle forearcs and restricted basin sediment reflect net crustal removal. (PDF p. 2)

### Figure 2

**Summary:** Sediment-unloaded basement-depth histories from drilling sites document forearc subsidence used to infer long-term trench retreat and tectonic erosion. (PDF p. 5)

### Figure 3

**Summary:** A world map locates the accreting and eroding subduction-zone segments included in the global compilation. (PDF p. 8)

### Figure 4

**Summary:** Common-scale cross sections compare the geometries of the study's accretionary plate margins. (PDF p. 9)

### Figure 5

**Summary:** Porosity-depth curves compare normally compacted sand and shale with accreted sediment and define the correction used to convert trench sediment into equivalent rock volume. (PDF p. 10)

### Figure 6

**Summary:** Common-scale cross sections compare the geometries and inferred crustal structure of nonaccretionary and erosive margins. (PDF pp. 12–13)

### Figure 7

**Summary:** Cross-margin data relate increasing orthogonal convergence rate to steeper forearc slope and taper, with clearer separation between accretionary and erosive regimes in slope. (PDF p. 14)

### Figure 8

**Summary:** Accretionary-margin data show forearc slope and taper decreasing as trench-sediment thickness increases. (PDF p. 15)

### Figure 9

**Summary:** Accretion rate rises with sediment thickness and delivery rate, while accretion efficiency decreases broadly with convergence rate and has little relation to sediment thickness alone. (PDF p. 16)

### Figure 10

**Summary:** Trench sediment becomes thinner as orthogonal plate-convergence rate increases. (PDF p. 17)

### Figure 11

**Summary:** Comparisons of forearc-erosion rate with convergence, sediment variables, and plate age reveal no simple first-order control on long-term erosion. (PDF p. 18)

### Figure 12

**Summary:** Deep-subduction flux is weakly related to convergence but separates accretionary and erosive margins when plotted against sediment-delivery rate because basement erosion dominates erosive budgets. (PDF p. 20)

### Figure 13

**Summary:** Assuming uniform arc magmatic productivity, plots against convergence rate and sediment thickness show net growth at accretionary margins but net loss at many erosive margins. (PDF p. 21)

### Figure 14

**Summary:** Arc melt production scaled by melting-column height produces implausible growth and erosion budgets for several accretionary and erosive margins. (PDF p. 23)

### Figure 15

**Summary:** Melt production scaled by convergence rate yields geologically more plausible budgets in which magmatism dominates accretionary growth and can outpace erosion in fast oceanic arcs. (PDF p. 23)

### Figure 16

**Summary:** Integrated margin budgets show growth at all accretionary and oceanic-arc margins but substantial net loss at several erosive continental margins. (PDF p. 24)

### Figure 17

**Summary:** The global input-output budget shows arc magmatism dominating new-crust addition while forearc erosion and sediment subduction return large crustal volumes to depth. (PDF p. 25)

### Figure 18

**Summary:** Comparing deep material subduction with arc productivity indicates that some erosive arcs could be supplied by recycled crust, whereas accretionary arcs require substantial new mantle extraction. (PDF p. 25)

## Forward summary

### Background and previous studies

1. Active margins were traditionally treated as sediment-accretion systems, but seismic surveys, drilling, subsidence, and exposure of forearc igneous and mantle rocks established widespread nonaccretion and basement erosion (Hussong and Uyeda, 1981; von Huene and Lallemand, 1990; von Huene and Scholl, 1991); this motivates classifying margins by net forearc-volume change over more than 10 Myr. (PDF pp. 1–3)
2. Earlier estimates that even accretionary margins subduct most incoming sediment, together with evidence for sediment in arc magma, make accretion efficiency essential to distinguishing shallow accretion from deep crustal recycling (von Huene and Scholl, 1991; Woodhead and Fraser, 1985; Tera et al., 1986; Plank and Langmuir, 1993). (PDF pp. 1–3)
3. Proposed erosion mechanisms include strong plate coupling, abrasion, and high fluid pressure, while subsidence and displaced paleodepth markers constrain trench retreat; this provides the basis for testing which tectonic variables actually control erosion (Hilde, 1983; von Huene and Lallemand, 1990; Lallemand, 1995, 1998; von Huene and Ranero, 2003). (PDF pp. 2–6)
4. Because active-margin magmatism is considered a major source of continental crust but published arc-growth estimates are lower than the loss calculated here, and because near-constant Phanerozoic freeboard implies slow growth, a revised magmatic budget is required (Dewey and Windley, 1981; Reymer and Schubert, 1984; Schubert and Reymer, 1985; Jacobsen, 1988). (PDF pp. 1, 21–22)
5. Subduction is the principal route returning continental material to depth, while isotopic models allow both extensive recycling and early rapid growth; therefore the combined sediment, basement, and magmatic mass balance determines whether continental volume can persist (Armstrong, 1971, 1981; Allègre and Rousseau, 1984; Taylor and McLennan, 1985). (PDF pp. 1, 22)

### Current study and results in figure order

#### Figure 1

**Schematics contrast accretionary margins, built from deformed off-scraped sediment, with erosive margins, where steep igneous or mantle forearcs and restricted basin sediment reflect net crustal removal.** (PDF p. 2)

This establishes the morphological end-members underlying the first takeaway and the paper's long-term net-volume classification.

#### Figure 2

**Sediment-unloaded basement-depth histories from drilling sites document forearc subsidence used to infer long-term trench retreat and tectonic erosion.** (PDF p. 5)

These histories provide observational support for the third takeaway by converting vertical subsidence and paleodepth change into estimates of landward trench retreat and removed forearc volume.

#### Figure 3

**A world map locates the accreting and eroding subduction-zone segments included in the global compilation.** (PDF p. 8)

The distribution supports the first and fifth takeaways by establishing the geographic basis for the conclusion that 57% of active margins are erosive and for the global mass balance.

#### Figure 4

**Common-scale cross sections compare the geometries of the study's accretionary plate margins.** (PDF p. 9)

The profiles supply the wedge dimensions used to estimate accumulated rock volume and long-term accretion rates, supporting the first and second takeaways.

#### Figure 5

**Porosity-depth curves compare normally compacted sand and shale with accreted sediment and define the correction used to convert trench sediment into equivalent rock volume.** (PDF p. 10)

This correction underpins the sediment-delivery and accretion-efficiency estimates central to the second takeaway.

#### Figure 6

**Common-scale cross sections compare the geometries and inferred crustal structure of nonaccretionary and erosive margins.** (PDF pp. 12–13)

Together with trench-retreat rates and crustal thicknesses, these geometries provide the eroded-basement volumes used in the third and fifth takeaways.

#### Figure 7

**Cross-margin data relate increasing orthogonal convergence rate to steeper forearc slope and taper, with clearer separation between accretionary and erosive regimes in slope.** (PDF p. 14)

The absence of erosive slopes below 3°, erosive margins below about 6.3 cm/yr, and accretionary margins above 7.6 cm/yr supports convergence rate as a first-order control in the first takeaway.

#### Figure 8

**Accretionary-margin data show forearc slope and taper decreasing as trench-sediment thickness increases.** (PDF p. 15)

This supports the first takeaway's secondary fluid-pressure mechanism: thick, fluid-rich sediment may reduce basal friction and permit shallower wedges.

#### Figure 9

**Accretion rate rises with sediment thickness and delivery rate, while accretion efficiency decreases broadly with convergence rate and has little relation to sediment thickness alone.** (PDF p. 16)

These relationships support the second takeaway: sediment supply controls how much is accreted, but rapid convergence reduces the fraction stripped from the downgoing plate.

#### Figure 10

**Trench sediment becomes thinner as orthogonal plate-convergence rate increases.** (PDF p. 17)

This connects the first two takeaways because faster plates spend less time in the high-deposition trench environment, linking convergence rate to both thin cover and low accretion efficiency.

#### Figure 11

**Comparisons of forearc-erosion rate with convergence, sediment variables, and plate age reveal no simple first-order control on long-term erosion.** (PDF p. 18)

The negative result directly supports the third takeaway and motivates the paper's interpretation that episodic ridge collisions dominate the best-documented high erosion rates.

#### Figure 12

**Deep-subduction flux is weakly related to convergence but separates accretionary and erosive margins when plotted against sediment-delivery rate because basement erosion dominates erosive budgets.** (PDF p. 20)

This supports the second and fifth takeaways: accretionary margins remain inefficient sediment filters, while erosive margins add large basement fluxes so sediment forms only 12–48% of their deeply subducted material.

#### Figure 13

**Assuming uniform arc magmatic productivity, plots against convergence rate and sediment thickness show net growth at accretionary margins but net loss at many erosive margins.** (PDF p. 21)

This first-pass balance supports the fourth and fifth takeaways while exposing the need to distribute melt production unevenly among arcs.

#### Figure 14

**Arc melt production scaled by melting-column height produces implausible growth and erosion budgets for several accretionary and erosive margins.** (PDF p. 23)

The failure of this scaling supports the fourth takeaway's rejection of melting-column height as the dominant global control.

#### Figure 15

**Melt production scaled by convergence rate yields geologically more plausible budgets in which magmatism dominates accretionary growth and can outpace erosion in fast oceanic arcs.** (PDF p. 23)

This supports the fourth takeaway by making magmatism 55–95% of growth at accretionary margins and explaining why rapidly converging oceanic arcs can grow despite erosion.

#### Figure 16

**Integrated margin budgets show growth at all accretionary and oceanic-arc margins but substantial net loss at several erosive continental margins.** (PDF p. 24)

This supports the fifth takeaway: oceanic-arc growth must ultimately compensate for losses from South America, Kamchatka, the Philippines, and other erosive continental systems.

#### Figure 17

**The global input-output budget shows arc magmatism dominating new-crust addition while forearc erosion and sediment subduction return large crustal volumes to depth.** (PDF p. 25)

This connects the second, fourth, and fifth takeaways by showing that eroded basement contributes about 55% of deeply subducted crust and that magmatism, not sediment accretion, supplies most new crust.

#### Figure 18

**Comparing deep material subduction with arc productivity indicates that some erosive arcs could be supplied by recycled crust, whereas accretionary arcs require substantial new mantle extraction.** (PDF p. 25)

This supports the fifth takeaway's conclusion that shallow recycling cannot dominate the global flux and that replenishment requires new extraction from the mantle.

### Discussion and interpretation

1. The authors interpret convergence rate as the dominant first-order control separating accretionary from erosive behavior, with sediment thickness and fluid release modifying wedge taper. This revises the historical accretion-dominated view and follows from the global distributions and correlations in Figures 3 and 7–10. (PDF pp. 8, 14–19, 26)
2. They conclude that accretion is an inefficient sediment filter: about 83% of sediment entering accretionary margins is deeply subducted. This strengthens the earlier estimate of extensive sediment bypass and is supported by the volume corrections and flux relations in Figures 4–5, 9, and 12. (PDF pp. 9–10, 16, 20–21, 26)
3. They infer that episodic collision of major ridges, rather than convergence, sediment supply, or plate age alone, produces the strongest long-term forearc erosion, while slow continuous erosion remains important. This evaluates the earlier coupling and abrasion hypotheses using the absence of correlations in Figure 11 and documented retreat accelerations at Tonga, Peru, Chile, and Costa Rica. (PDF pp. 18–20, 26)
4. They argue that long-term arc melt production is controlled more plausibly by convergence rate than by melting-column height and must average about 90 km³ Myr⁻¹ km⁻¹ to maintain existing crust. This addresses the mismatch between earlier arc-production estimates and crustal survival, using the failed Figure 14 budget and the more realistic Figures 15–16 balance; it also limits stable oceanic arcs to combinations such as crust below 36 km at 8 cm/yr convergence and 3 km/Myr retreat. (PDF pp. 21–27)
5. They conclude that tectonic erosion and sediment subduction recycle a modern-crust-equivalent volume every 2.2 Gyr, requiring oceanic arcs to grow and later accrete to continents while substantial continental material returns beyond the arc roots. This closes the background mass-balance problem through Figures 16–18: erosive continental margins lose crust, oceanic arcs supply compensating growth, and mantle-derived magma dominates addition of new material. (PDF pp. 24–27)
